figures.headline: DeepTutor's overview shows static course grounding and dynamic learner memory feeding both tutoring and question generation in a closed cycle.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 2, DeepTutor unifies two tutoring tasks through a shared Hybrid Personalization Engine: problem tutoring, which produces citation-grounded, learner-calibrated guidance $a$ for a student question $q$, and question generation, which produces customized practice items for a topic $\tau$ targeting the learner’s gaps.

citing_sentences: Therefore, we construct TutorBench to close this gap: every entry explicitly couples a detailed learner persona with source-grounded knowledge gaps and an interactive tutoring task, as illustrated in Figure 3.

A single agent loop drives every capability (Chat, Solve, Mastery Path, and the extensions of this section), while cross-surface memory (raw event traces, per-capability summaries, and cross-surface synthesis over the Trace Forest and learner profile), pluggable knowledge-base engines, installable skills, consultable sub-agents, and accumulated personal context are shared across all of them. Every extension reuses this substrate instead of instantiating a separate learner model.

citing_sentences: Figure 5 summarizes the loop: a benchmark entry initializes the learner profile, source-grounded gaps, task, and materials; the simulator converts the gaps into first-person beliefs, conducts multi-turn tutoring, and then requests customized practice; the resulting traces are judged with personalized rubrics.
Figure 5 in the main paper summarizes the full interactive evaluation loop used for TutorBench; this appendix provides the implementation details.

abstract: Education is one of the most promising real-world applications for Large Language Models (LLMs). However, current LLMs rely on static pre-training knowledge and lack adaptation to individual learners, while existing RAG systems fall short in delivering personalized, guided feedback. To bridge this gap, we present DeepTutor, a fully open-source agentic framework that unifies citation-grounded problem tutoring with difficulty-calibrated question generation. A hybrid personalization engine couples static knowledge grounding with dynamic learner memory, continuously adapting each interaction to the student’s evolving needs. The same personalization substrate further extends to adaptive learning workflows, interactive books, and proactive multi-channel tutoring agents. To evaluate personalized tutoring, we introduce TutorBench, an interactive benchmark incorporating customized learner profiles grounded in university-level curricula across five domains. We further propose an LLM-based first-person interactive evaluation protocol that conducts assessments via a profile-driven student simulator. Complementary evaluations on established benchmarks, supported by human-alignment and ablation studies, confirm the framework’s robustness and general utility. Results show that DeepTutor improves personalized metrics by 10.8% on average and strengthens general agentic reasoning across five backbone models by 29.4%.

sections.body: The introduction argues that tutors diagnose misconceptions and pose targeted practice, while current systems handle these tasks separately. Tutoring workflows diagnose student errors within one turn, and question generators follow predefined objectives rather than student traces. The authors state that current systems lack a fine-grained, evolving model of the learner. They propose DeepTutor, which links problem tutoring and question generation through a shared trace forest, and TutorBench, a student-centric benchmark with first-person interactive evaluation across five university-level disciplines.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing tutoring and question-generation workflows run in isolation, so tutoring traces do not shape later practice items.

sections.body: Course material is indexed as a knowledge graph and a dense embedding index, and retrieval results are fused with reciprocal rank fusion. Learner memory is a Trace Forest whose trees have three levels, from session summaries to tool outputs and validation outcomes. Three memory agents update a profile with three views: session history, an inventory of weaknesses, and pedagogical self-reflections. Problem tutoring runs in three stages: investigate, guided step-by-step solving, and evidence-based iterative writing. Question generation separates idea selection from question, answer and explanation construction, and a validator that shares no reasoning chain with the generator checks the output.
sections.heading: DeepTutor Framework
sections.headline: A shared personalization engine feeds problem tutoring and question generation, and every completed interaction updates the learner profile.

sections.body: The section treats the Hybrid Personalization Engine as a fixed set of shared parts: one agent loop, cross-surface memory built on the Trace Forest, pluggable knowledge-base engines, installable skills, consultable sub-agents, and accumulated personal context. Table 1 maps each extension to a capability runtime, a learning surface, or a deployment level. The Book Engine composes sources, prior interactions and capability outputs into an interactive book and flags pages when source knowledge drifts. Partners run the same capabilities as persistent multi-channel agents. The authors state that effects on retention, engagement and learning outcomes require longitudinal human studies.
sections.heading: Extending the Personalization Substrate
sections.headline: Extensions such as Deep Research, Mastery Path and the Book Engine reuse one personalization substrate, while quantitative evaluation covers only the tutoring core.

sections.body: Each profile is built from sampled source pages and carries three generated knowledge gaps: misconceptions, incomplete understanding, and missing knowledge. Each gap is anchored to specific source pages and paired with a correct understanding that is reserved for judging and not shown to tutor systems. Interactive tasks pass rejection sampling for gap coherence, task-gap fit and conversational naturalness. Annotators then review profiles and tasks for factual correctness and gap-task consistency before release. Tasks cover concept understanding, problem solving, application and comparison, and every retained entry carries three source-grounded gaps.
sections.heading: TutorBench
sections.headline: TutorBench pairs 90 learner profiles from 30 knowledge bases in five disciplines with 270 source-grounded interactive tasks.

sections.body: Evaluation uses a first-person protocol in which an LLM student simulator, built from each entry's profile and gaps, runs multi-turn tutoring and requests practice. Gemini-3-Flash powers the simulator and all tutor backbones, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 judges transcripts on ten metrics, each scored from 1 to 5. Each transcript is scored three times and the scores are averaged. DeepTutor improves overall quality by 10.76% over Naive Tutor, while the four baselines cluster closely. The largest tutoring-side gains are in Vividness, Personalization and Logical Depth. Overall quality varies by 0.16 points across the five domains.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: DeepTutor reaches 3.91 overall quality on TutorBench against 3.53 for the Naive Tutor baseline.

sections.body: Personalization work includes reflective summarization, accumulated user models, RAG-style adaptation and hierarchical agent memory, and the authors build a tree-structured dynamic memory on these lines. Classical learner modeling is covered through knowledge tracing, from Bayesian knowledge tracing to neural and memory-based variants. Among LLM-based educational systems, the section cites conversational tutors with student modeling, multi-agent pedagogical architectures and open-source platforms. It notes that existing benchmarks measure open-ended pedagogical quality, while adaptive tutoring grounded in individualized materials remains underexplored. The authors unify explanation and question generation through a shared learner model.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work covers LLM memory, knowledge tracing and LLM tutors, and finds adaptive tutoring on individualized materials underexplored.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the framework, the TutorBench benchmark with source-grounded profiles and a first-person simulator, and the reported cross-domain stability and human-LLM preference trends. It states that the solver-only transfer study yields a 29.4% average gain across five backbone families. It reports that ablations show knowledge grounding and learner memory complement each other, anchoring what the tutor says and shaping how it adapts. It suggests that the same substrate supports adaptive workflows, interactive books and proactive agents as a path toward long-horizon personalized learning systems.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: DeepTutor improves overall quality by 10.8% on TutorBench and yields a 29.4% average gain across five backbone families.

sections.body: The authors note that LLM-powered student simulators and rubric-based assessors differ from real learner behavior, and that validation with human students could be considered. The multi-stage pipeline trades additional inference cost for stronger controllability and personalization. TutorBench could be scaled to finer-grained courses, longer curricular trajectories and larger learner populations. The Book Engine and Partners are presented as architectural instantiations, and their effects on retention, engagement, interruption cost and real learner outcomes require longitudinal human studies. A broader impacts note warns that LLM tutors can produce hallucinated facts and asks that generated content be treated as assistive.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Interactive results rest on LLM simulators and rubric judges, and the extensions' effects on real learners remain untested.

sections.body: Appendix A expands related work on tool-augmented agents, LLM memory, knowledge tracing and educational agents. Appendix B gives the closed-loop algorithm and the TutorBot loop, which runs a bounded ReAct-style tool-calling loop. Appendix C lists the PDF sources for the 30 knowledge bases and describes task generation with rejection sampling. Appendix D covers the first-person evaluation details, the temperatures of 0.3 for the solve module, 0.7 for the question module and 0.5 for the personalization module, and the backbone models run with greedy decoding at temperature 0.0.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists extended related work, implementation details, TutorBench construction, evaluation protocol, hyperparameters and backbone models.
